---
title: "Conflict"
pagetitle: "Conflict — Christopher W. Blair"
---

*How do counterinsurgency policies affect rebel and civilian behavior? How do the transnational dimensions of conflict shape the micro-dynamics of civil wars?* This work explores the consequences of investments in state capacity, the efficacy of combatants' efforts to build civilian support, and the resilience of militant groups under repression.

**Militant alliances.** A central contribution is the [Militant Group Alliances and Relationships (MGAR)](data-mgar.qmd) dataset, documenting 7,409 dyad-year relationships among 2,613 militant groups from 1950 to 2016. With Erica Chenoweth, Michael C. Horowitz, Evan Perkoski, and Philip B.K. Potter, I show that shared ideology — and shared religion in particular — helps militant organizations sustain cooperation under the shadow of state repression, even though shared state sponsorship (an established alternative commitment device) is far rarer than militant cooperation itself ([*IO* 2022](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0020818321000114)). With Horowitz and Potter, I find that leadership decapitation — especially the killing of a group's founder — triggers alliance breakdown by weakening targeted groups, raising fears about operational security, severing personal ties between leaders, and inducing command-and-control problems ([*JOP* 2022](https://doi.org/10.1086/715604)). And with Potter, I show that groups like al-Qaeda and the Islamic State build large transnational alliance networks as a strategic response to material or ideological deficits, trading operational capability for ideological credibility and vice versa ([*JOGSS* 2023](https://doi.org/10.1093/jogss/ogac035)).

**Refugees and conflict.** In work with David van Dijcke and Austin L. Wright ([forthcoming at the *American Economic Review*](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3885937)), I leverage historical returnee settlement patterns and previously unreleased combat records to estimate the causal effect of a large cash-assistance program for refugee returnees on conflict in Afghanistan. Policy-induced return had cross-cutting effects: it reduced insurgent violence — plausibly by raising reservation wages and discouraging labor-intensive combat — while increasing social conflict, an effect significantly offset by kinship ties and access to informal dispute-resolution institutions.

**Counterinsurgency policies.** Can state forces use reparations to mitigate civilian backlash to wartime harm? Using declassified microdata on U.S. payments to civilians wrongfully detained in Iraq (2004–2008), I find that detainee-release payments are robustly associated with reduced insurgent violence — effects that were greatest in mixed and Sunni areas, for attack types most prone to civilian informing, and when release was paired with other population-centric reforms to detention ([*JCR* 2022](https://doi.org/10.1177/00220027221080118)).
